1:
The witnesses take up the psalm's title before its first cry, treating the note "when he fled from Absalom his son" as the key that unlocks all that follows. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry calls the inscription a key hung ready at the door: composed as David fled his rebel son (the story of 2 Sam. 15), the psalm was meditated by a man in great grief, who went up the Mount of Olives weeping, his head covered and his feet bare, and yet "wept and prayed, wept and sung, wept and believed," sowing in tears. Henry will not let David's flight be mistaken for cowardice; true Christian fortitude, he says, lies more in a gracious serenity of mind than in daring enterprises with sword in hand, and he remembers that this trouble was the very evil God had threatened to raise up against David out of his own house for the matter of Uriah (2 Sam. 12:11).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses that providential irony: "How publicly does God take vengeance for the sins which David committed so privately!" In the horror of the revolt he reads the adultery of Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah come home, and Nathan's word fulfilled, "The sword shall not depart from thy house." Clarke notes too that the hearts of all Israel went after Absalom (2 Sam. 15:13), so that the inscription itself proves the psalms are not arranged in chronological order, and he traces the word mizmor to a root meaning "to cut," whether cut into syllables for the music or cut on wood for the singers.

On the swelling number of the enemies the witnesses gather. The reformed John Gill hears David amazed that his own son should seek his life and that subjects he had ruled with clemency should rebel; Henry likens Absalom's faction to a snowball strangely gathering as it rolls, and warns that princes must not build too much on their interest in the people (Ps. 146:3). Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, fills in the scene from the history: Ahithophel counselling a pursuit of twelve thousand, and Hushai flattering Absalom to gather all Israel from Dan even to Beersheba, as the sand which is by the sea for multitude. Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, title it a "Morning Hymn of One in Distress, but Confident in God," set after the two prologue psalms and sharing the "holy hill" with Psalm 2; the notion that it is an evening hymn, they say, rests on a grammatical misconception.

Two voices lift the verse clean off its history. The latin-fathers Augustine reads the whole psalm in the Person of Christ, taking the undutiful son for the undutiful disciple, so that when the Son of God forsook the mind of Judas and the devil entered his heart, Christ may be said to have fled his face — Absalom, he adds, meaning in the Latin tongue a father's peace. The reformed John Calvin, though he holds firmly to the Absalom occasion drawn from the psalm's whole tenor, is blunt that the titles themselves are "destitute of authority," mere marginal glosses of the Jews, and finds the truest mark of David's faith in his daring to pour his complaint freely into God's bosom. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon closes the swell where Henry began it, at 2 Sam. 15:12, "the conspiracy was strong," and observes that troubles always come in flocks, for "sorrow hath a numerous family."
2:
From the number of his foes David turns to the sharpest thing they say, a taunt aimed not at his body but at his soul, that there is "no help for him in God." The reformed John Gill notes that the words are spoken to his soul as much as of it — cutting words that reached his very heart like a sword. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the malice in three strokes: the enemies put a spiteful construction on his troubles, as Job's friends did on Job, concluding that God had abandoned his cause; they blasphemously reflected on God as unable to relieve him; and they laboured to drive him to despair. A child of God, Henry says, startles at the very thought of despairing of help in God; and so David spreads the taunt before the Lord as Hezekiah spread Rabshakeh's letter, praying, they say there is no salvation for me in thee, but, Lord, do thou say unto my soul, I am thy salvation (Ps. 35:3). The reformed John Calvin hears the same pride: the enemies' boldness grew because they were confident David had been rejected by God, Absalom hoping for victory from his own power and making no account of the God who had so often delivered his king.

The verse closes on the first Selah, and here the witnesses openly divide over a word Ellicott calls the puzzle of ordinary readers and the despair of scholars. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott insists it can carry no ethical or spiritual sense — it occurs seventy-one times across thirty-nine psalms and thrice in the ode of Habakkuk, and "for ever," the old Rabbinic gloss, will not fit them; nor is it a mere strophe-mark, since it falls even in the middle of a stanza. It must be a musical term, he concludes, most probably a direction to play loud, from a root meaning "to raise," though he owns that others derive it from a word meaning "to be silent" and make it the very opposite. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees it is a musical note, bidding the singer lift the voice, make a pause, or lengthen the tune, yet marks that it always stands at some remarkable passage and so quickens the attention of singer and hearer alike. Adam Clarke, of the same school, weighs both derivations — sal, to elevate the voice, or salah, to spread out and meditate — and, with Fenwick, Parkhurst, and Dodd, leans to the second, reading Selah as a nota bene, "attend to this," a sense he finds confirmed where higgaion stands beside it in Ps. 9:16. Henry lands there too: "Selah — mark that, or, stop there, and consider a little." So the debate is genuine, whether the word is a bare musical rubric or a summons to the mind, and the witnesses leave it unresolved.
3:
Against the taunt that God will not help him David sets his threefold confession of what God is, and the witnesses divide the verse among its three images. On the first, the reformed John Gill hears the soldier in David, who so often borrows the language of war: the Lord is "a shield for me," or about me, the same protection faith still holds up in Christ's blood and righteousness against the law, the accusing conscience, and Satan. Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, render it more exactly "a shield behind me," covering him behind and before, and trace the confession to its fountain-head in Gen. 15:1 (cf. Deut. 33:29); Charles Ellicott presses the same "behind me," a guard against the emissaries of Absalom now on his track. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon will have it wider still — not a shield only but a buckler round about, a defence above, beneath, within and without.

On the second image the witnesses turn from safety to honour. Keil observes the paradox at its sharpest: David's kingdom is taken from him, yet Jahve is his glory; with covered head and dejected face he climbed Olivet (2 Sam. 15:30), and just there calls God his glory and the lifter of his head. Ellicott hears in the phrase an echo of Horace's "O thou my guard and my sweet honour," set against the same picture of the humiliated monarch muffled and barefoot under Shimei's curses. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps it plain — "my glory" is the occasion of David's glorying in God's power and favour — and Gill adds that God is the true honour of all whom he owns.

The third image gathers the other two into hope. Adam Clarke, of the wesleyan-arminian school, reads "the lifter up of mine head" as spoken prophetically, a sure knowledge that God would restore him to the state his enemies had cast him from, a confidence so settled that he could lie down and sleep expecting the divine protection. Wesley agrees: God will restore him to his former power and dignity. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole verse into the three great things God is to his people — safety, for he is a shield about them; honour, for the crown may fall from the head and God still be their glory (Isa. 60:19); and joy and deliverance, for he lifts up the head both out of trouble and under it, so that they do not droop. Spurgeon names the same trio with a preacher's cadence — "defence for the defenceless, glory for the despised, and joy for the comfortless." The witnesses hardly divide at all; where they differ, it is only over whether the shield stands behind David against his pursuers or round about him on every side.
4:
Turning from what his enemies say to what he himself has done, David looks back on a prayer already heard, and the witnesses read the verse as a settled experience of answered crying. The reformed John Gill takes the crying for prayer, and vocal prayer at that — the Targum renders it simply "I prayed" — for though God hears the language of the heart when no voice is uttered, as with Hannah, here the loudness marks the ardour and importunity of a man in earnest. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the comfort out: care and grief do us good and no hurt when they set us praying, and when the earnestness of the voice comes from the fervency of the heart it is noticed in the account, that we cried unto God (cf. 1 Sam. 1:13).

On the answer "out of his holy hill" the witnesses attend to the place. Henry recalls that David had ordered Zadok to carry the ark back into the city (2 Sam. 15:25), knowing that God was not tied to the ark of his presence, and that no distance could fix a gulf between the communications of God's grace toward us and the operations of his grace in us; the answers came from the holy hill because Christ was set King upon the holy hill of Zion (Ps. 2:6), through whom our prayers are heard. Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, take the hill for Zion and read the verse as a retrospect on the past night's safety, a pledge now in the morning that the God who supported him will hear again. But the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "his holy hill" otherwise — not Zion but heaven itself, so called, he says, in Ps. 15:1. Charles Ellicott, keeping to the grammar, notes only that "with my voice" means aloud, and that the verbs are present, expressing the habit of the royal psalmist.

Adam Clarke, of the wesleyan-arminian school, gathers the encouragement of the closing Selah: David was exposed to danger and had need of fervour, and though his enemies said and his friends feared there was no help for him, he heard me out of his holy hill. Mark this, Clarke urges, and take encouragement from it, for God never forsakes those who trust in him, and never shuts out the prayer of the distressed. The witnesses agree that the prayer was heard; they part only over whether the hill from which the answer came is the earthly Zion of the ark or the heaven above it.
5:
"I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me" — and the witnesses hear in that plainest of sentences the calm of a man who has cast his cares on God. The reformed John Gill weighs two ways of reading the sleep: some, with Jarchi, take it for the heavy slumber that grief can bring, as it fell on Elijah and Jonah and the disciples in the garden; but Gill himself prefers the serenity of a mind at peace, David laying himself down and sleeping quietly amid his troubles, a very blessing of life from the Lord. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way — he slept securely, casting all his cares on God, and awaked after a sweet and undisturbed sleep. Adam Clarke sharpens the wonder of the waking: humanly speaking there was every reason to fear that David might be murdered in his bed, since his own servants had been corrupted by his son, yet the God who was his shield preserved him, so that he both slept and awaked and his life was still whole in him. He who knows that God is his protector, Clarke says, may go quietly to his rest, fearing neither fire nor sword nor wicked men nor malevolent spirits.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, fix the Hebrew against those who would make it a resolve to sleep — the form is a backward glance, "and thus I then fell asleep" — and find the ground of the waking in the last clause: it is because Jahve supports him, his very hand the pillow under David's head. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon presses the faith in it: anxiety would have kept David on tiptoe watching for the enemy, but faith let him lie down and sleep in the midst of trouble, surrounded by foes, for "so he giveth his beloved sleep"; and the quietness of a heart thus stayed on God, he adds, is a higher work than the natural resolution of manly courage, being the gracious operation of God's own Spirit.

Matthew Henry, of the same puritan-evangelical school, opens the verse three ways: to the common mercy of every night, for which we ought to give thanks each morning, since many lie down and never wake, like the firstborn of Egypt, while we wake to another day because the Lord sustained us; to the singular calm of David's spirit, whom the treachery of his son and subjects never robbed of an hour's sleep; and, with some of the ancients, to the resurrection of Christ, who slept the sleep of death and awaked the third day because the Lord sustained him, that he should not see corruption. The witnesses do not divide over the peace of the verse; they differ only in tracing the sleep now to the exhaustion of grief, now to the rest of faith.
6:
His rest taken, David rises to defy the multitude, and the witnesses read his fearlessness as the fruit of the faith just shown. The reformed John Gill remembers that David had been a man of courage from his youth — the lion and the bear at the sheepfold, Goliath in the valley, and all his later exploits of war — so that though thousands were now in arms against him, his own son at their head and all the tribes revolting, with only a few friends about him, he was not dismayed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts the reason in a sentence: strength and numbers are nothing against the omnipotence of God, and he who has made God his refuge has no cause to fear. Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, notes only that the enemies "set themselves" — that is, arrayed themselves as for battle (cf. 1 Kings 20:12).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the change that faith has wrought in the man. No one seemed less safe, for his enemies were numerous, spiteful, and resolute, set against him round about, thousands against one, having prevailed so far that they seemed already to have gained their point; and yet no one was more secure. Henry sets the verse beside David's earlier word to Zadok, when, sending back the ark, he had spoken doubtfully like a humble penitent — "let him do to me what seemeth to him good" (2 Sam. 15:26) — whereas now, like a strong believer, he speaks confidently and has no fear concerning the event. A cheerful resignation to God, Henry concludes, is the way to obtain a cheerful satisfaction and confidence in God. Charles Spurgeon, of the same school, guards the courage from bravado: David does not underestimate the number or the wisdom of his foes, reckoning them at ten thousands and viewing them as cunning huntsmen who would hem him in as hunters ring a deer; yet, buckling on his harness for the day's battle and looking them in the face, he trembles not and is ready for the fight.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, carry the thought straight into the prayer that follows, for the fearlessness of this verse is what emboldens the cry "Arise, O LORD" in the next. The witnesses do not divide here; together they show a man who, having slept under God's wing, can wake to face an army, and whose refusal to be afraid is not the daring of the sword-hand but the quiet of a heart persuaded that the battle is the Lord's.
7:
The psalm's one stroke of imprecation follows hard on the resolve not to fear — "Arise, O LORD; save me, O my God" — and the witnesses take first the prayer and then the ground it stands on. The reformed John Gill notes that God can seem, to his people's apprehension, as if asleep, so that they call on him to arise; and he hears behind the word the ancient cry of Moses when the ark set forward (Num. 10:35). For all his tranquillity of mind David does not neglect the means of safety but prays, and pleads his covenant interest, addressing God as his own God. Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, mark the same boldness in that "Arise," taken from the mouth of Moses, for God is said to arise when he takes a decisive part in what happens in the world. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the pastoral lesson: though God had undertaken David's defence, his continued protection hung on continual prayer and faith, for God never ceases to help so long as we pray, and when our hands hang down and we restrain prayer our enemies prevail.

On the second half the witnesses differ over the tense of the deliverance. Clarke reads "thou hast smitten" as a confident future — "thou wilt smite" — David speaking as sure of the victory as if he already had it. Ellicott likewise would render the perfects as presents, "thou smitest... breakest." But the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the words as a backward look at deliverances already given: God had often broken the power and restrained the malice of David's enemies, had smitten Saul and the Philistines upon the cheek-bone and broken their teeth, and it is good, when the enemy seems strong, to remember how often God has broken him before. So the difference is real — whether the verse recalls past mercies or seizes a future one by faith — though all agree on what the smiting means.

For the imagery the witnesses are one. Charles Ellicott conceives the enemies as wild beasts, the lion and the bear of David's own youth, whom God renders harmless; the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the smitten cheek-bone as a mark of contempt and reproach, and the broken teeth as the shattering of their strength and the instruments of their cruelty, likening them to beasts of prey. Clarke agrees that to break the jaws and teeth is to confound an adversary utterly, treating him with the contempt one shows a dog. Charles Spurgeon gathers the comfort of it for every believer: God has broken the teeth of the ungodly, so that let them say what they will their toothless jaws cannot devour — "thou hast to do with a dragon whose head is broken, and with enemies whose teeth are dashed from their jaws." The witnesses leave the verse as a prayer half answered before it is finished, the cry for rescue resting on a God who has already disarmed the foe.
8:
"Salvation belongeth unto the LORD" — the psalm ends where its confidence has been tending, on a maxim the witnesses treat as its crown. The reformed John Gill unfolds it as the confession of the whole Trinity's work: salvation, temporal and eternal alike, is the Lord's — resolved by the Father, who chose men to it and covenanted with his Son; wrought by Christ, the author of eternal salvation; and applied by the Spirit, who convinces men of their need of it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears David's faith grown triumphant, closing in exultation the psalm he had begun in complaint: two great truths hold him up, that salvation belongs to the Lord, whose prerogative and property and promise it is to save, so that all who have him for their God are sure of it; and that "his blessing is upon his people," pronounced upon them so surely that, whatever reproaches men heap on them, they are blessed indeed by the God who can command a blessing. Charles Spurgeon presses the first clause hardest of all, calling it "the sum and substance of Calvinistic doctrine," salvation by grace from first to last — not of him that willeth nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy — and finds in the second the speciality of that grace, a blessing resting not on Egypt or Tyre or Nineveh but on God's own chosen and blood-bought people.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that God alone saves, the fountain whence all help comes, and that his blessing both saves his people and keeps them saved; and he reads the closing Selah as a double nota bene — that salvation comes from God, and is continued by God. Clarke draws the whole psalm together as he ends: three strains of complaint, confidence, and petition, in which David, deserted and railed on, opposes to the multitude of his foes the one God, "But thou, O LORD"; and, as a good king should, remembers even his rebel subjects in his prayer, "thy blessing be upon thy people."

Over that last clause, though, the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott parts from the rest. It is not, he insists, the statement of a fact but an intercessory prayer — better rendered "let thy blessing be upon thy people" — and in that generous petition for the very people who had risen against him he finds the mark of the true Shepherd, a close that, as Ewald said, throws a bright light on the depth of David's noble soul. So the witnesses divide gently at the end: whether the final words pronounce a blessing already resting on God's people, as Henry and Gill and Clarke take it, or breathe a last prayer that it may rest on them, as Ellicott would have it. Keil and Delitzsch let the verse stand as it is, salvation the Lord's and the blessing his people's, and the psalm closes on its third and final Selah.
